rejected.title: Demand
card: Demand is how much of a product buyers want and can afford at each price. Wanting something is not enough. A buyer must also be able to pay for it.
As the price of a product rises, people usually buy less of it. As the price falls, they usually buy more.
Buyers cut back when prices rise for two reasons. Some cannot afford it any more, and some switch to a cheaper product instead.
A demand schedule is a table that lists the quantity buyers would purchase at each price. A demand curve is a line that shows the same thing on a graph, and it slopes down.
rejected.remember: Demand links price to the amount people buy: a higher price usually means less is bought.

a.q: A shop in Hobart lowers the price of its sandwiches. What will most likely happen to the number of sandwiches buyers want?
opts: It will usually rise
It will usually fall
It will stay exactly the same
It will rise only for rich buyers
a.why: Demand says that as price falls, people usually buy more. Lower prices make the sandwiches affordable to more buyers, and some will switch from other lunches. The idea is not limited to rich buyers.
a.clue: Think about what a lower price does to what buyers can afford.

b.q: Ava in Perth would love a new $900 phone but has only $300 saved. Which statement about her is correct?
opts: She wants the phone, but she is not part of demand at $900
She wants the phone a lot, so she is part of demand at $900
She plans to save for it, so she is part of demand at $900
Phones are popular, so she is part of demand at $900
b.why: Demand needs buyers who both want a product and can afford it at that price. Ava wants the phone but cannot pay $900, so she is not part of demand at that price. Wanting it a lot, or planning to save, does not change what she can pay now.
b.clue: Demand needs more than wanting a product.

problems.detail: The right option is the only one not starting 'She shows demand because...', so a student can spot the odd one out without knowing the idea.
'It is not part of her demand' is awkward and unclear. Demand belongs to the market at a price. Better: 'She wants the phone, but she is not part of demand at $900.'

a.q: A Hobart shop cuts the price of its sandwiches. What usually happens to the number of sandwiches people want to buy?
opts: It usually goes up
It usually goes down
It stays about the same
It goes up for wealthy buyers alone

a.clue: Think about what a lower price does to what buyers can afford.

b.q: Ava in Perth really wants a new phone that costs $900, but she has $300 saved. Is she part of the demand for that phone at $900?
opts: No, as she cannot pay that price now
Yes, as she wants the phone very much
No, as she has not been to a shop yet
Yes, as she could save the rest later
b.why: Demand needs buyers who both want a product and can afford it at that price. Ava wants the phone but cannot pay $900, so she is not part of demand at that price. Wanting it a lot, or saving later, does not change what she can pay now.
b.clue: Demand needs more than wanting a product.

b.best: No, as she cannot pay that price now
